title: Print your first greeting
description: Use print and text blocks to make the computer show a message.
steps: Find the print block and its text block in the workspace.
Change the text to Hello, learner! and predict the output.
Run your program and check the exact words.
Change the greeting to include your name, run again, and submit your blocks.
expectedResult: The output shows the greeting exactly once, including your changes.
evidenceBrief: Submit your greeting program and explain which block displays the text.

title: Put instructions in order
description: Connect print blocks to build an ordered sequence.
steps: Choose a three-step everyday task, such as washing your hands.
Connect three print blocks, each with one instruction.
Predict the order, then run the program and read its output.
Swap two instructions, observe the difference, then restore the correct order and submit.
expectedResult: Three instructions appear in the same order as the connected blocks.
evidenceBrief: Submit your ordered program and describe what changed when you swapped blocks.

title: Build a number calculator
description: Use arithmetic blocks as the input to a print block.
steps: Replace the greeting text with an arithmetic block set to addition.
Put the numbers 7 and 5 into the arithmetic inputs.
Predict the result and run the program.
Change addition to subtraction, predict again, and compare the output before submitting.
expectedResult: 7 + 5 prints 12; changing the operator to subtraction prints 2.
evidenceBrief: Submit your calculator and record the expected and actual results for both operators.

title: Calculate a rectangle's area
description: Turn a simple formula into connected Blockly blocks.
steps: Plan the formula area = length multiplied by width.
Connect a multiplication block with inputs 6 and 4 to print.
Run the program and compare its result with your prediction.
Change the inputs to 3 and 5, retest, and explain the two inputs in your submission.
expectedResult: The two tests print 24 and 15.
evidenceBrief: Submit your area program, both test results and an explanation of the formula.

title: Compare two numbers
description: Explore comparisons and true or false results.
steps: Place a comparison block inside print.
Set the comparison to 8 greater than 3, predict, and run.
Change it to 2 greater than 3 and run again.
Test equality with two identical numbers and explain all three results.
expectedResult: The comparisons produce true, false and true respectively.
evidenceBrief: Submit your comparison program and describe when the result becomes true.

title: Repeat a message
description: Replace repeated instructions with a repeat loop.
steps: Place a print block showing Go! inside a repeat block.
Connect the number 4 as the repeat count.
Predict the number of output lines and run your program.
Test counts 1 and 0, then explain how repetition changes the output.
expectedResult: Count 4 prints Go! four times, count 1 once, and count 0 produces no printed lines.
evidenceBrief: Submit your loop and record the three counts with their observed output.

title: Store and use a variable
description: Give a value a name and use it in another instruction.
steps: In Variables, create a variable called learnerName.
Set learnerName to the text Amani before the print instruction.
Use the learnerName value block as the input to print, then run.
Change the stored value to another name and explain why the print block does not need to change.
expectedResult: The print instruction shows the currently stored name.
evidenceBrief: Submit your variable program and explain the difference between the variable name and its value.

title: Find and fix a sequence error
description: Compare expected output with actual output and debug the order.
steps: Connect print blocks to show Finish, Start and Build in that order.
Run the program and compare it with the intended order Start, Build, Finish.
Move the blocks into the intended order and run again.
Submit your corrected program and explain the original fault and your retest.
expectedResult: The corrected output reads Start, Build, Finish on separate lines.
evidenceBrief: Submit the corrected blocks, expected and actual results, and the change that fixed the fault.

title: Count with a changing variable
description: Use a variable and repetition to create a counter.
steps: Create counter and set it to 1 before a repeat loop.
Repeat five times: print counter, then change counter by 1.
Predict the output and run the program.
Move the change instruction before print, compare the result, then restore and submit.
expectedResult: Printing before the change produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
evidenceBrief: Submit your counter and explain why the position of the change instruction matters.

title: Generate a multiplication table
description: Combine a counting loop, variables and arithmetic.
steps: Create a for loop with a variable i counting from 1 to 5 by 1.
Inside it, print i multiplied by 3.
Predict all five results, then run and compare.
Change the multiplier to 4 and submit your program with both test cases.
expectedResult: Multiplier 3 prints 3, 6, 9, 12, 15; multiplier 4 prints 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.
evidenceBrief: Submit your table generator and the predictions and results for both multipliers.

title: Make an if-else decision
description: Choose a message using a comparison and two branches.
steps: Create score and set its value to 70.
Build if score is at least 50, print Target reached; otherwise print Keep practising. Use the if block controls to add else.
Test score values 70, 30 and 50.
Submit your blocks and explain the boundary case at 50. This is a programming exercise, not a competency award.
expectedResult: Scores 70 and 50 print Target reached; score 30 prints Keep practising.
evidenceBrief: Submit your decision program and record results above, below and at the boundary.

title: Combine two conditions
description: Use boolean logic to decide when two requirements are met.
steps: Create two boolean variables: hasKit and isReady.
Print Start when hasKit AND isReady are true, otherwise print Check requirements.
Test all four combinations of true and false.
Change AND to OR, compare the outcomes, and explain the difference.
expectedResult: AND permits Start only when both values are true; OR permits it when either is true.
evidenceBrief: Submit your program and a four-case test record for the two operators.

title: Build a running total
description: Accumulate values through a loop.
steps: Create total and set it to 0 before a for loop.
Count i from 1 to 5 by 1 and change total by i on each repetition.
Print total after the loop, then predict and run.
Extend the loop to 10, retest, and explain why total is initialised outside the loop.
expectedResult: Adding 1 through 5 gives 15; adding 1 through 10 gives 55.
evidenceBrief: Submit your accumulator and explain its initial value and both test results.

title: Read values from a list
description: Store several readings and retrieve a selected item.
steps: Create a variable readings and set it to a list containing 12, 18 and 24.
Print the length of readings, then retrieve and print its second item.
Predict the output before running the program.
Add a fourth reading, retest the length, and explain how the list differs from a single number.
expectedResult: The initial list has length 3 and its second item is 18; adding an item changes the length to 4.
evidenceBrief: Submit your list program and explain the length and the chosen item's position.

title: Stop a while loop safely
description: Use a changing condition to end repetition.
steps: Create count, set it to 0, and build a while count is less than 3 loop.
Inside it, print count and change count by 1.
Predict the output, run and explain why the loop stops.
Temporarily remove the change instruction to observe the execution limit, then restore it and submit the fixed program.
expectedResult: The working loop prints 0, 1, 2 and stops; the faulty loop is stopped by the runner's limits.
evidenceBrief: Submit the terminating loop and describe the fault, the guard and your correction.

title: Create a reusable function
description: Name a reusable sequence and call it more than once.
steps: In Functions, define a function called showSteps.
Inside it, print Plan, Build and Test in order.
Call showSteps twice from the main program and predict the output.
Change the function once, run again, and explain why both calls use the revised sequence.
expectedResult: The three-step sequence appears twice, with both calls reflecting changes to the definition.
evidenceBrief: Submit your definition and calls, plus an explanation of how reuse reduces duplication.

title: Use a function input and return value
description: Generalise a calculation using a parameter.
steps: Define a function with a return value called doubleNumber and add an input n using its controls.
Return n multiplied by 2.
Print calls with inputs 3, 0 and -2, predicting each result first.
Submit your blocks and explain how the input changes while the function stays the same.
expectedResult: Inputs 3, 0 and -2 produce 6, 0 and -4 respectively.
evidenceBrief: Submit your function, three tests and an explanation of its parameter and returned result.

title: Classify a number with branches
description: Design and test mutually exclusive branches.
steps: Define classifyNumber with input n and a return value.
Use if, else if and else to return Positive, Zero or Negative.
Print calls for -5, 0 and 5 and test all branches.
Explain why the branch order and the equality check avoid an incorrect classification.
expectedResult: -5 gives Negative, 0 gives Zero, and 5 gives Positive.
evidenceBrief: Submit your classifier and a test for every branch, including zero.

title: Simulate a sensor decision
description: Model a robotics decision with simulated readings; no hardware is connected.
steps: Create a distance variable representing a simulated reading in centimetres.
Build if distance is below 10, print Stop; otherwise print Move.
Test distances 5, 10 and 20 and record the results.
Add a branch for negative readings that prints Invalid reading. Explain the difference between this model and a real sensor.
expectedResult: 5 gives Stop; 10 and 20 give Move; a negative reading gives Invalid reading.
evidenceBrief: Submit your simulation, four test cases and an explanation of its hardware limitation.

title: Design and test your own Blockly solution
description: Combine variables, decisions, repetition and a reusable function in an independent project.
steps: Choose a text-based problem such as a supplies calculator or a simulated alert system, and state the expected behaviour.
Plan and build a Blockly solution with at least one variable, decision, loop and function.
Test a normal case, a boundary case and an unexpected input; fix a fault and retest.
Submit your blocks, output, test record and an explanation of one design choice. Ask your teacher for review.
expectedResult: The program meets your stated behaviour and your test record shows how you checked it.
evidenceBrief: Submit your complete Blockly project, three test cases, the fault and retest, and a short design explanation.
